text:
“Yes,” said Bai, “a stirring day—a day well spent.” He went on chattering animatedly: about the dancing—what a sight, those village children—and the “ladies”—“Miss Julie,” a fine girl in boots, a spirited girl—and Marie—well—we shall see what she has been up to ... I know her....

The other two did not speak. Neither of them was listening, either. It was so quiet that they could hear their own footsteps on the ground. At the end of the avenue, the cemetery’s iron gate rose up with its great cross.

“But Bai,” said Katinka.

“Do you think there are ghosts here?” said Bai. He opened the side gate.

They went in. At the gate, Katinka took Huus’s arm. The cemetery lay in the twilight like a large garden. Roses and box hedges and jasmines and lindens gave off a heavy fragrance, and gray and white stones rose between the hedges.

Katinka held Huus’s arm very tightly as they walked.

Bai went ahead. He trotted along the shrubbery, flinging out his arms as if he meant to flush out chickens.

Katinka stopped: “Just look.”

A clearing had been cut through the trees, so that one could look down across the fields to the fjord. The twilight hovered like a veil over the darkly gleaming surface of the water, still and dreamlike.

It was silent, as though life had died away beneath the fragrant air ... Motionless, they stood close against one another.

Slowly they walked on. Katinka stopped from time to time and read the inscriptions on the stones that shone out in the twilight. She read them, names and years, in a soft and trembling voice.

“Loved and missed.”

“Loved beyond the grave.”

“Love is the fulfillment of the law.”

She stepped closer and lifted the branches of the weeping willow: she wanted to read the name on the stone.

Then there was a rustling behind the willow.

“Huus,” she said, clutching his arm convulsively.

Something fled away over the wall.

“It was a couple of people,” said Huus.

“How frightened I was,” said Katinka, holding her hands to her breast.

She continued to walk close against him while her heart pounded.

They spoke no more. Now and then there was a rustling in the shrubbery, and Katinka started.

“My little friend, my little friend,” Huus whispered as if to a child. Katinka’s hand trembled beneath his.

Bai stood at the end of the path.

“Are you there?” he said.

He opened the gate. It clapped shut in its iron hinge behind them.

Out in the avenue, Bai took Huus aside:

“It is a damned scandal,” he said ... “that such a thing should #exist#—a desecration of the holy place ... Kiær had told me ... what it was like—with those scoundrels....

“But damn it, I didn’t think it was possible....

“Not even to have any feeling for death—the Garden of Death—ugh, damn it....

“Devil take me, one can’t even be left in peace on the benches....”

Huus could have struck him.

       *       *       *       *       *

They came down through the streets. The booths stood closed and deserted. Here and there, by a solitary streetlamp, a tradesman was gathering up his wares.

The din from taverns spilled into the street. Sleepy and with heads bowed, people drifted home in pairs.

Marie appeared in the hotel gateway. She was heavy with sleep and weary.

Katinka waited by the carriage. All around them horses were being harnessed and carriages driven away. The “Nightingales” sang loudly out into the courtyard,

They took their seats. Bai wanted to drive and sat with Marie.

    Oh you—my Valdemar!
    I love you....

“They keep at it,” said Bai.

They drove through the night; past the woods; out across the flat fields.

Marie, asleep, hung bent over the basket in her lap. Huus and Katinka sat in silence, staring out at the countryside. Now and then Bai spoke.

“Ho, ho—my beasts—

“Come now—so slowly—”

And it grew quiet as before.

Bai wanted “a little pick-me-up” and managed to rouse Marie until she found a bottle of port.

“Will you have some?” he said.

“No—thank you,” said Huus.

“That’s damned wrong.” Bai took the bottle from his mouth. “A stomach has to have something against the cold of the night.”

Bai took another swig. “That is something one learns in the field,” he said.

He began to talk about the Prussians and the war.

“Good-natured people,” he said, “taken one by one—great eaters—terrible gluttons—but good hearts—really good hearts—one by one—but in the #corps#—the devil take them....”

No one answered. Marie nodded off again.

Katinka only wished that he would be quiet.

“But terrible eaters,” Bai said again.

He began to grow patriotic and spoke of old Denmark and a bloody banner. Then he lapsed into silent reflections when no one answered.

Only the clatter of the horses in their harness could be heard. Now and then a cock crowed across the fields.

“Put the shawl on,” said Huus. “It is cold.”

Gently he laid the blue shawl around Katinka’s shoulders.

Little by little, day dawned over the fields.

       *       *       *       *       *

“I suppose there’ll be breakfast,” said Bai. They were home and stood at an ungodly hour on the steps in the gray morning.

“Yes, if you like,” said Katinka.

But Huus had to go home. It was high time.

“Well,” said Bai, “as you wish.” He yawned and went inside. Marie had been dragged away with the baskets.

Huus and Katinka were left alone. She leaned against the doorpost. They were silent for a moment.

“Then thank you for today,” she said. It came softly and uncertainly.

“As though it were not I who should be thanking you.” It came as an outburst, and in an instant Huus had seized her hand and kissed it twice, three times, with hot lips.

And then he was in the carriage and gone.

“What the devil came over him?” said Bai, coming outside. “Is he gone?”

Katinka stood in the same spot. “Yes,” she said, “he drove away.”

She steadied herself against the door and quietly went inside.

       *       *       *       *       *

Katinka sat by the open window. Day had broken. Larks and all the birds exulted above the broad meadow. The summer fields were filled with song and sunshine and twittering.




IV


The chained dog slept in the hot courtyard and would not be roused. A pair of scoured tubs had been set out to dry in the sun.

Katinka opened the hall door; only the humming of the flies could be heard through the bright, cool rooms.

She went through the garden room and out into the garden. There was not a soul there, and it was utterly silent. On the croquet lawn, balls and mallets lay abandoned. The rosebushes drooped in the heat.

“Is that you, dear Mrs. Bai?” It came in a half-whisper from the summerhouse, and Mrs. Linde nodded: “Yes, Linde is reading his sermon, you know.

“They are all out in the back garden—the Kiærs came, you see, a whole wagonload of them with their guests ... And it is inconvenient, of course, when Linde is reading his sermon....”

“Are the Kiærs here?” said Katinka.

“Yes ... they came here for coffee—they are in the back garden—and the new doctor too ... And you, who have been to the fair ... Huus told us about it.”
